Syllabus

CSS 553 · Software Architecture · Spring 2027draft

Vitals

  • Course Number and Title: CSS 553: Software Architecture
  • Description: Concepts, representation techniques, development methods, and tools for structuring software systems: architectural styles and connectors, quality attributes and tactics, architecture description and standards, domain-specific architectures and product lines, distributed and service-based architectures, and architecture decision-making. Students inherit a running distributed system, recover its architecture, and design and implement its evolution.
  • Meeting Time/Place: TBD (planned as Monday/Wednesday, 2-hour sessions).
  • Credit: 5 units. This translates into 10–11 hours of work per week outside of class.
  • Notice: Contents of this Syllabus and the course web site can change at any time in the term.
  • Class Culture:
    • Excellence: I have high standards. You are expected to meet them.
    • Initiative: Ask questions! Engage and wrestle with the material, your colleagues, and myself.
    • Grace: Freedom to learn and grow. Extend courtesy to each other.

Texts & Supplies

Required texts:

Code Text Access
B Bass, Clements & Kazman, Software Architecture in Practice, 4th ed. (Addison-Wesley, 2022) UW Library, free
EAI Bass, Lu, Weber & Zhu, Engineering AI Systems: Architecture and DevOps Essentials (Addison-Wesley, 2025); assigned chapters only (Session 14) UW Library (O'Reilly), free

Course text (CT): chapters written for this course and shared with CSS 555 and CSS 478, on the course web site. They cover what Bass does not: connectors, the style catalog, REST, distributed data, microservices, evolution patterns, ML- and LLM-enabled systems, architecture recovery, ADRs, product lines. Where an assigned book explains a topic, the chapter is a companion: a worked example on the course system, pitfalls, and exercises.

Papers: listed in the schedule; PDFs on Canvas.

Additional resources:

  • Khononov, Balancing Coupling in Software Design (Addison-Wesley, 2024): one coupling model (strength, distance, volatility) for modules and services
  • Newman, Monolith to Microservices (O'Reilly, 2019): patterns for evolving a running system
  • Ford, Richards, Sadalage & Dehghani, Software Architecture: The Hard Parts (O'Reilly, 2021): decomposition, distributed data, and contracts in service-based systems
  • Kleppmann & Riccomini, Designing Data-Intensive Applications, 2nd ed. (O'Reilly, 2026): replication, consistency, streams
  • Kästner, Machine Learning in Production: From Models to Products (MIT Press, 2025), open access: ML-enabled systems from requirements to operations
  • Skelton & Pais, Team Topologies (IT Revolution, 2019): team structure and Conway's law

If you need a text in an alternative format, contact DRS Accessible Instructional Materials at printdrs@uw.edu; conversion can take 4–6 weeks, so request early.

Topics and Learning Objectives

Topics: what architecture is (structures, views, decisions); components, connectors, configurations; architectural styles; quality attributes, scenarios, and tactics; usability-supporting architecture; architecturally significant requirements and Attribute-Driven Design; evolving a running system (strangler fig, branch by abstraction, parallel run); architecture description, ADLs, and ISO/IEC/IEEE 42010; REST; interfaces and integration; ML- and LLM-enabled systems; distributed data; microservices and platforms; lightweight evaluation; architecture recovery, conformance, and debt; product lines and domain-specific architectures; the architect in the organization.

Learning Objectives: By the end of this course, students will:

  1. Define and compare architectural concepts, styles, and connectors using standard terminology.
  2. Recover the as-built architecture of a running system and explain its drift from the as-intended architecture.
  3. Specify quality requirements as quality-attribute scenarios and utility trees, including usability scenarios supplied by a UX team.
  4. Select and justify styles, patterns, and tactics against those scenarios, recording each decision as an ADR.
  5. Design an architectural evolution with Attribute-Driven Design and evolution patterns, and document it in views that conform to ISO/IEC/IEEE 42010.
  6. Derive REST from its constraints and analyze consistency and availability tradeoffs in distributed data.
  7. Integrate an ML or LLM component into an architecture and analyze the tradeoffs it introduces (cost, latency, testability, safety, privacy).
  8. Implement an architectural increment with AI-assisted development while keeping architecture decisions your own.
  9. Evaluate a design with a lightweight evaluation and manage its architecture debt.
  10. Synthesize a published architecture paper and present it to a technical audience.

Course Structure

Act Weeks Theme Core Question
I 1–2 Structure What is the architecture, and how did the system we inherited drift from it?
II 3–5 Qualities Which qualities matter, and which tactics deliver them?
III 6 Method How do we design and describe an evolution?
IV 7–8 Distribution and AI Components What changes when parts talk over a network, or when one of them is a model?
V 9–10 Evolution How do we keep an architecture healthy over time?

Session format (with some variation): standup (~10 min, Weeks 3–10), lecture (~60 min), ICA (~30 min), paper presentations (Weeks 7–9).

The course system. The course works on one system all quarter: the UWB social network built by CSS 553 in Spring 2026, running on the course platform (Docker Swarm, gateway, registry, monitoring). It arrives with an evaluation: risk themes, debt hotspots, and a threat model from CSS 555 (Winter 2027) teams that studied it. In parallel, CSS 478 (Usability and User-Centered Design) teams research its users and test its interfaces. See the schedule for dates.

Requirements

Pre-Class Activities (PCA): Readings listed in the schedule are due before the session they are listed under. Sessions with assigned reading have a short Canvas reading quiz, due at the start of class.

In-Class Activities (ICA): Structured team exercises with rotating roles (recovering a service's box-and-line diagram, writing scenarios from incidents, choosing tactics, reviewing ADRs). Submitted on Canvas by the end of class; graded on completion and good-faith effort.

Course Project: See Course Project.

Paper Presentation: Pairs (separate from project teams) present one software architecture research paper from a recognized venue (ICSE, FSE, ICSA, ECSA, or similar; at least 7 pages), 10 minutes per pair: Student A (4 min) context, problem, approach; Student B (4 min) architectural contribution, evidence, takeaway for practitioners; 2 min Q&A. Slides carry diagrams, charts, and figures only. Each student is graded on their own segment. Sign up by Week 3; presentations open Sessions 13–18.

Midterm: In class, Session 10, 90 minutes, closed book, one one-sided handwritten reference sheet. Covers Sessions 1–8.

Final Exam: Finals week, 120 minutes, cumulative, closed book, one double-sided handwritten reference sheet. The final exam is mandatory to pass the course.

Course Project

Inherit, evaluate, evolve. Teams of 3–4 inherit two or three services of the course system and the platform contracts they run under (one deploy.sh, openapi.yaml, ADRs per service). Over the quarter each team recovers what it inherited, decides what to change, builds it, and hands the result to the next offering.

Partner teams. Each team with a user-facing service is paired with a CSS 478 team. The partner supplies usability scenarios (Week 4), prototypes (Week 6), and test findings (Week 8); your team supplies a running increment and test accounts (Week 7). Your grade depends on what you do with what you receive, never on your partner's work. If there is no partner, the instructor supplies scenarios and teams test each other's increments.

Evaluation lead. Students who took CSS 555 take this role in their team: they run the team's lightweight evaluation and own its fitness functions.

AI features. Evolution goals may include an AI-powered feature (for example moderation, feed ranking, or summaries). A team that adds one treats the model as a component like any other: its own scenarios (cost, latency, failure, unsafe output), ADRs for how it is integrated, and fitness functions that watch it.

Milestone Deliverable Due Points
G0 Inheritance report: as-built vs. as-documented architecture of your services, reconstructed ADRs for the three most consequential past decisions, top five risks with evidence (from the inherited evaluation where one exists) Sun Apr 11 20
G1 Quality drivers: utility tree with at least 10 scenarios (including your partner's usability scenarios), ASR list, prioritized evolution goals (features and risk paydown) Sun Apr 25 25
G2 Evolution design: ADD iteration record, C&C, module, and deployment views, interface changes as openapi.yaml diffs, at least three new ADRs, fitness functions specified, response to partner prototypes Sun May 9 50
G3 Increment: running increment deployed on the platform, fitness functions in CI, dashboards for your scenarios' response measures, test accounts for your partner Sun May 16 25
G4 Final package: lightweight evaluation of your services (utility tree, risks, sensitivity and tradeoff points), an ADR answering every partner finding, debt register, demo, handoff README for the next offering, AI-use account Presentations Wed Jun 2; package Sun Jun 6 80
Total 200

Milestones are due at 11:59 PM PT. Each milestone includes a short statement of who contributed what.

Rebuild clause. If G0 shows an inherited service cannot carry the evolution, the team may declare it a rebuild with an ADR that cites the evidence. Platform contracts stay.

Testing rules: load, fault, and security tests target only your own services on the course platform or a local deployment, never another team's services without that team's agreement, and never public UW systems.

Make-Up and Late Policy

Deliverables are due at the stated date and time. Late work loses 10% per day; the maximum grade for any late submission is 90%.

Lowest score drops: 2 reading quizzes, 2 ICAs. Milestones are not dropped.

Exams: no make-up exams except in documented exceptional situations. No electronic devices during exams; pen, pencil, scratch paper, and a handheld calculator (not a phone) are permitted.

Exceptions: Extensions are granted for documented health issues, bereavement, university business, and legal obligations. Request an extension before the deadline whenever possible; requests made after the fact require documentation of why advance notice was impossible.

Extra Credit

None.

AI Policy

AI coding tools are expected for implementation. You are the architect; AI is your engineering team. Your grade reflects the quality of your architectural decisions, not the volume of your code.

  • Yours: scenarios, decisions and ADRs, views, evaluation findings, presentations, exam answers. An ADR you cannot defend in a standup counts as not written.
  • Disclosure: G3 and G4 state which tools you used, what for, where they helped, and where they introduced drift from your design.
  • Safety: commit before letting an agent change files; review every generated file against your views; verify that AI-suggested dependencies exist; never commit secrets.

Collaboration & Academic Integrity

  • Project: teams share work freely internally. Inherited artifacts (Spring 2026 code, ADRs, and the CSS 555 evaluation) are the starting point; cite them, and mark every ADR as inherited or new.
  • Partner teams: CSS 478 scenarios and findings are inputs you cite, not work you submit as your own.
  • Paper presentations: each student presents their own segment.
  • Exams: individual work only.
  • Not permitted: submitting another student's or team's architecture work as your own; submitting AI-generated architecture documents you cannot explain.

Suspected violations are referred under the UW Student Conduct Code, which describes your rights and the appeal process.
